title: Judgment Is the Job Now
author: Lead With Kelly
summary: This article argues that AI has commoditized the analytical and production skills that defined high performance in corporate careers -- market research, synthesis, deck construction, benchmarking -- and exposed what was always the actual differentiator: independent judgment. The author opens with a vivid scene of a senior leader who couldn't answer "what do you actually think we should do?" after presenting a flawless six-week analysis, and frames this as the moment AI made the deficiency visible rather than created it. The article traces historical analogs (industrial revolution, automation, software transitions) to argue this is a pattern, not a disaster, before turning to what the author calls the development problem nobody is solving: the traditional pipeline for building senior leader judgment -- having junior people do the deep analytical work for years -- is disappearing, and companies that depend on AI for productivity without building alternative judgment-development pathways will find themselves with a missing generation of senior leaders. The article describes the profile of the emerging high performer: comfortable with incomplete information, forms strong views quickly, uses AI as a thinking partner not a producing partner, and spends more time on the question than the answer.
points: * The question that separated capable leaders from stagnant ones has always been 'what do you actually think we should do?' -- AI just made that question unavoidable, because it removed the analysis as a hiding place for leaders who could produce but not decide. * Every major technological transition has commoditized the skill that defined the previous era's high performer; knowledge workers assumed they were exempt from this dynamic, but they were not and never were. * The core development problem is structural: junior people historically built judgment by doing the analysis -- pattern recognition came from hundreds of hours staring at messy data -- and that training ground is disappearing without most companies designing a replacement. * The new high performer profile is identifiable: enters meetings and asks the question no one else thought to ask, points immediately to the unexamined assumption in an analysis, uses AI to challenge their own recommendation rather than produce a deliverable. * Companies that use AI purely for productivity gains while severing the analytical pipeline that developed the next generation of leaders will find themselves with a missing cohort of senior leaders in five years -- the companies that figure this out first will have a meaningful competitive advantage.
quotes: Judgment was always what separated leaders who got stuck from leaders who got promoted. AI just makes it visible faster, because the analysis is no longer the differentiator.

She looked completely self-assured. She knew every detail. And she did. But she was outsourcing the judgment that should come with leadership positions. In her mind, the details were the work. Not the call.

The information gathering, the synthesizing, and the framing, all of it can be done quickly and inexpensively now. The cover has been removed, and a new question looms over every senior career: Are you capable of independent thinking, or are you merely adept at producing?

Pattern recognition came from spending hundreds of hours staring at messy data. Strategic instinct came from being deep in the weeds long enough to feel where the real levers were. Executive presence came from presenting your work in rooms where senior leaders ripped it apart and you had to defend it. The execution layer wasn't just the work. It was the training ground.
The next generation of leaders won't be developed by accident, the way we were. They can't. The path you took doesn't exist anymore. New ones have to be designed. This is our job as senior leaders.
They use AI as a thinking partner, not a producing partner. They don't ask it to write the email. They ask it to challenge the recommendation they're about to make.

The companies that figure this out first will end up with a meaningful advantage. The leaders five years from now will not get there the way you got there. They can't. The path you took doesn't exist anymore.
